idiom_name: view-model struct owning the behaviour + a consumer-supplied html/template fragment
implementation_notes: Go has no component runtime, no render props and no stateful UI tree, so the closest honest realization is the server-rendered split: a struct (or small package) owns the state and behaviour - validation, transitions, formatting - and the consumer supplies the markup as an html/template template the struct is executed into; the package documentation describes html/template as 'a specialized Template ... that produces a safe HTML document fragment', and a template may be executed safely in parallel. What replaces prop getters is the template calling explicit methods on the view model ({{.Expanded}}, aria-expanded="{{.AriaExpanded}}") instead of receiving a grab-bag of attributes, so the invariant stays in Go and is testable without rendering. Where a UI toolkit with callbacks exists (WASM or desktop bindings), the render callback must be explicit - Go re-renders nothing by itself.
pitfalls: Template sets must be parsed before first execution ('cannot Parse after Execute') and shared sets must be treated as read-only after startup, or concurrent executions race.
Handing a template a mutable struct invites markup to mutate behaviour through method calls: expose read-only accessors and keep transitions behind explicit methods.
html/template escapes by context, so a template author who reaches for template.HTML to 'fix' output silently opens an injection hole.
